analysis.one_liner: Automatically raises the federal minimum wage each year with the cost of living.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the federal minimum wage law so that the wage rate adjusts automatically every January, using the same cost-of-living formula that sets Social Security benefit increases. Without indexing, Congress must pass a new law each time it wants to raise the minimum wage, which has historically happened only sporadically, allowing the wage to lose value to inflation in between. This bill would have made those adjustments automatic starting in 1993.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage would gain, because their pay would keep pace with rising prices automatically instead of eroding between the occasional congressional pay raises. This workforce is concentrated in retail, food service, and other low-paid service jobs. Future Congresses would also be spared repeated political fights over the wage floor.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so the minimum wage is adjusted each year in the same manner as Social Security benefits are indexed to the cost of living [S2] [S3].
The adjustment takes effect with calendar years beginning 1993, and the Secretary of Labor would make the adjustment at the start of each year [S3].
Automatic indexing means the wage floor no longer loses value to inflation during the years Congress does not act, protecting the buying power of the lowest-paid workers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers — concentrated in retail, restaurants, and other labor-intensive services — would bear higher annual payroll costs as the wage rises automatically with prices. Some of that cost could show up in prices for consumers or in reduced hours for low-wage staff.

drawbacks.text: Indexing makes wage increases automatic rather than debated, so in a downturn Congress could not easily hold the wage floor steady without passing new legislation; employers with thin margins would face payroll costs that rise every year whether or not business conditions allow [S2].

Because the adjustment follows the Social Security cost-of-living formula, the increase depends entirely on how that index measures inflation, and it could raise the wage in years when the broader economy is weak [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For minimum-wage workers, automatic indexing is the most durable way to protect a wage floor, since it removes the need to win repeated political fights. The cost falls on low-wage employers and, to some degree, consumers through prices, and automatic increases give policymakers less flexibility in a weak economy. On balance the bill's benefits are targeted at the lowest-paid workers and the costs are diffuse; its main design question is whether inflation adjustments alone are enough, since indexing preserves but does not raise the wage's real value.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of the Congress, referred to committee, then sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a floor vote before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Representative George Miller of California introduced the bill on September 30, 1992, near the end of the two-year Congress [S1] [S5].
Nine other members joined as cosponsors — eight Democrats and one Independent — including Representative William Ford of Michigan, then the chairman of the committee it was sent to [S4] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced [S5].
About a week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where it stayed; no further action appears in the record before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers are better off, because the wage floor will not rise automatically with inflation; the minimum wage will instead stay flat until Congress passes a separate raise. Low-wage workers lose the buying-power protection the bill would have provided.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders, and the bill received no recorded floor action, so no vote shows how the chambers would have split; the bill simply died in committee [S3] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have raised the wage floor every year with inflation, increasing payroll costs for restaurants, retail, and other businesses that rely on minimum-wage labor. Blocking it let those employers keep a wage floor that loses value to inflation between congressional raises.
Workers paid at or near the federal minimum would have kept their buying power automatically. They are the intended beneficiaries of the bill.
